title: HumanUP: Separating “Discover a Get-Up” from “Make It Deployable”
content_lines: Sources: [arXiv:2502.12152](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12152) · [pinned official code](https://github.com/RunpeiDong/HumanUP/tree/7516e0f27e6f4d1e7365cf64ea577a78247bd8cb)

Review scope: the complete fifteen-page paper and reward/training appendix, plus official G1 discovery, tracking, curriculum, and safety-penalty code. Simulation success, repeated hardware trials, and unaddressed fall safety are kept separate.

> In one sentence: Stage I discovers fast contact-rich get-up under weak regularization and simplified collision, then Stage II tracks an 8× slower trajectory with full URDF, randomized posture and terrain, and strong control constraints; G1 achieves 78.3% get-up and 98.3% roll-over across six surfaces, with explicit snow and slope failures.

Key terms include fall recovery (跌倒恢复), getting-up policy (起身策略), motion discovery (动作发现), trajectory tracking (轨迹追踪), contact-rich task (接触丰富任务), sim-to-real curriculum (仿真到现实课程), posture randomization (姿态随机化), control regularization (控制正则化), safety score (安全分数), and full collision geometry (完整碰撞模型).
## Engineering problem

Getting up is not periodic locomotion. Arms, knees, hips, and torso make unknown contact, and early progress may reduce body height. A final-standing reward is sparse. Adding low speed, torque, and smoothness from the start can prevent discovering any contact sequence.

This resembles discovering a rescue route and paving it simultaneously. Requiring every unexplored route to be smooth and speed-limited may leave no route; first find a traversable path, then slow it and add guardrails.

Collision geometry is crucial because the whole body contacts the floor. A simplified body may succeed in simulation while expecting contacts absent in reality. The paper shows such a policy still looks good under full-URDF simulation evaluation yet fails all five flat-ground hardware trials.
## Method

Stage I uses sparse task and soft-symmetry reward, simple collision, one initial posture, flat terrain, and weak regularization, allowing a sub-second motion. Supine reward includes height, height progress, uprightness, feet, force progress, and symmetry; prone recovery first rolls to supine.

Stage II tracks rather than rediscovers. Get-up is interpolated to eight seconds and roll-over to four, with full URDF, 20k supine and 20k prone postures, randomized terrain/dynamics, and strong torque, speed, action-rate, and posture penalties. Task learning becomes easier while deployment conditions become harder.

Observation is 868-dimensional: 74 proprioceptive values, ten history steps, and 54 online-adaptation latent values, with 23 actions. Linear velocity and yaw are deliberately omitted because they are unreliable after a fall.
### Input → processing → output

G1 has 29 actuated DoF; three wrist DoF are disabled, leaving 23. Discovery and tracking use PPO, Isaac Gym at 1 kHz, and low-level PD at 50 Hz. The appendix reports about 5B Stage-I steps, 4096 environments, and a single RTX 4090 or L40S.

Postures are generated by randomizing a canonical lie, dropping from 0.5 m, and simulating ten seconds to resolve collision. Supine and prone each have 20k poses split in half. Stage II randomizes flat, rough, and sloped terrain plus CoM and delay. Four-times slowdown has excessive torque, while ten-times does not converge; eight is empirical.
Evaluation includes success, action and DoF jerk, energy, and torque/DoF safety scores at threshold δ=0.8 with equal peak and duration weighting. Feasibility and deployability are distinct.
## Key figures
![Figure 1: real-world recovery](../assets/humanup-2502.12152/figure-1-real-world.jpg)
Figure 1 demonstrates supine get-up, prone roll-over, and surfaces. It is capability evidence; repeated success is in Figure 3.
![Figure 2: two-stage curriculum](../assets/humanup-2502.12152/figure-2-two-stage.jpg)

Figure 2 separates discovery and tracking while changing collision, posture, regularization, speed, and domain. The key is converting sparse search into dense tracking before adding reality constraints.
![Table I: simulation ablation](../assets/humanup-2502.12152/table-1-simulation.jpg)

Table I reports 95.34%, 94.40%, and 92.10% for supine, roll-over, and complete prone recovery. A baseline gets 92.62% supine but action jitter 5.39 versus 0.56 and energy 650.19 versus 91.74, and is not deployable. One-stage training fails entirely.
![Figure 3–4: hardware counts and curriculum failure](../assets/humanup-2502.12152/figure-3-hardware.jpg)

Figure 3 has ten trials each on concrete, brick, tile, mud, about 10° grass, and snow. Full get-up is 78.3%, roll-over 98.3%, and manufacturer get-up 41.7%. Figure 4 shows one-stage height stopping around 0.4 m.
## Decisive evidence

The strongest evidence combines full-URDF ablation with repeated hardware tests. Simplified-URDF policies score 93.95%, 87.73%, and 89.59% in simulation but fail 5/5 on real flat ground, isolating contact-geometry mismatch.
Ten trials on six surfaces are stronger than a video, while explicit snow and slope failures bound the claim. A 78.3% rate is progress, not autonomous reliability.
## Paper-to-implementation mapping

At commit `7516e0f27e6f4d1e7365cf64ea577a78247bd8cb`, `simulation/legged_gym/legged_gym/envs/g1waistroll/g1waistroll_up.py::G1WaistRollHumanUP` implements discovery. `_update_standing_prob_curriculum`, `_update_regularization_scale_curriculum`, and `_reward_*` implement task and regularization curricula.

`simulation/legged_gym/legged_gym/envs/g1rolltrack/g1waistroll_track.py::G1WaistRollTrack` loads and interpolates discovery motion. `_reward_tracking_dof_error`, `_reward_base_roll_gravity_error_cosine`, and torque/limit/energy functions implement deployable tracking.
## Limits and evidence boundary

The authors explicitly note possible incompatibility between discovered motion and strong Stage-II constraints, dependence on high-frequency physics, reward hacking such as unnatural arm raising, and limited stairs or uneven-terrain study.

Independent limitations include policy handoff from prone roll to supine get-up, one robot with ten trials per terrain, qualitative disturbance tests, and no autonomous fall detection, post-impact health inspection, or repeated-fall thermal statistics.

Automatic get-up does not make falling safe. Before activation, check people, obstacles, joints, motors, workspace, communication, and stop. Unknown postures should request assistance rather than force recovery.
## Bounded engineering takeaway
Separate sparse contact search from sim-to-real regularization. Discovery finds a feasible sequence; tracking slows, smooths, randomizes, and verifies it under full contact geometry.
For crawling or rolling, discover multiple candidates and select by torque, collision, time, and transfer rather than locking Stage II to the first local optimum.
## Reproduction checklist

Pin URDF/collision, simulator, discovery and tracking configuration, interpolation, posture sets, terrain, randomization, commit, and seeds. Reproduce one-stage, no Stage II, simple URDF, no posture randomization, and hard-symmetry ablations across seeds.
Hash posture generation and test 4×/8×/10× trajectories for tracking, torque, speed, jerk, energy, and success. Sweep geometry, friction, delay, CoM, and soft ground.

Stage hardware from suspended signals and canonical mat trials to randomized lie, roll, and surfaces. Log success, partial, fallback, torque/current, temperature, collision, and stop. Production needs fall detection, workspace and health state machines, and human takeover.
> **Engineering judgment:** the difficult part is first discovering an effective contact sequence without hardware constraints, then proving that slowing and regularizing it did not close the route.
